module.title: Relations
module.description: Binary relations on a set; the four core properties (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive); equivalence relations and their classes; partial and total orders; Hasse diagrams.

lessons.title: Relations and Their Properties
lessons.welcome: A RELATION is just a set of ordered pairs — but with that simple definition we can express prerequisite chains, friendship graphs, and database joins. Three properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) classify almost all the relations you'll meet.
objectives: Define a binary relation as a subset of A × B.
Recognize when a relation is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, or transitive.
Use a directed graph or matrix to represent a relation.
Decide whether a given relation has each property.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: What's the difference between a function and a relation?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Every function IS a relation, but not vice versa. A function requires every input to have exactly ONE output. A relation imposes no such restriction — it can pair an input with multiple outputs, or with none.

flow.title: Binary relation
flow.content: A **binary relation** R from A to B is a subset of A × B. We write `a R b` for `(a, b) ∈ R`. A **relation on A** is a subset of A × A.

flow.title: Relations around campus
items: **Prerequisite relation** at KAU: (CPCS 203, CPCS 222) ∈ R if CPCS 203 is a prerequisite of CPCS 222.
**Enrollment relation:** (student, course) ∈ R if the student is enrolled.
**Friendship on social media:** symmetric (if A is friends with B, then B is friends with A).
**Following on X/Twitter:** NOT symmetric (you can follow without being followed back).
**'Same Saudi region as':** reflexive, symmetric, transitive — an equivalence relation.

flow.title: Four core properties (relation R on A)
items: **Reflexive:** ∀a ∈ A, (a, a) ∈ R. Every element relates to itself.
**Symmetric:** ∀a, b ∈ A, (a, b) ∈ R → (b, a) ∈ R.
**Antisymmetric:** ∀a, b ∈ A, ((a, b) ∈ R ∧ (b, a) ∈ R) → a = b.
**Transitive:** ∀a, b, c ∈ A, ((a, b) ∈ R ∧ (b, c) ∈ R) → (a, c) ∈ R.

flow.title: Symmetric vs antisymmetric — NOT opposites
flow.content: A relation can be both symmetric AND antisymmetric (only the diagonal {(a, a)} satisfies both at once). Or neither (e.g., a relation with (1, 2) ∈ R, (2, 1) ∈ R, but 1 ≠ 2 fails antisymmetric, and missing some self-pairs fails symmetric).

flow.title: Property check on standard relations on ℤ
Representing a relation
items: **Directed graph:** vertices = elements of A; draw an arrow from a to b if (a, b) ∈ R.
**Matrix:** M_{ij} = 1 if (aᵢ, aⱼ) ∈ R, 0 otherwise.
**Set of pairs:** {(a, b) | …} listed explicitly.

flow.title: Reading the matrix for properties
rows: Off-diagonal: at most one of M_{ij}, M_{ji} is 1
If M_{ij} = 1 and M_{jk} = 1, then M_{ik} = 1 (close under composition)

flow.trigger: After the property checks — students confuse antisymmetric with 'not symmetric'.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: If a relation is antisymmetric, does that mean it can't be symmetric?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: It can — but only on the diagonal. The relation R = {(a, a) | a ∈ A} is BOTH symmetric AND antisymmetric. Antisymmetric means: whenever both (a, b) and (b, a) hold, then a = b. If only diagonal pairs exist, this is automatic.

flow.title: Property check on a small relation
flow.problem: A = {1, 2, 3}. R = {(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)}. Determine which of the four properties R has.
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive: need (1,1), (2,2), (3,3) all in R. ✓
Symmetric: (1,2) ∈ R needs (2,1) ∈ R ✓. No other off-diagonal pairs. ✓
Antisymmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) both in R but 1 ≠ 2. ✗
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting to check (a,a) → (a,a) → (a,a) for transitivity (these are automatic but appear in formal verification).

flow.title: Property check on '<' over ℤ
flow.problem: Determine which of the four properties the strict less-than relation '<' has on ℤ.
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive: a < a never. ✗
Symmetric: 1 < 2 but not 2 < 1. ✗
Antisymmetric: vacuously true — there are no pairs (a, b) with both a < b and b < a. ✓
Transitive: a < b and b < c ⇒ a < c. ✓
flow.common_mistake: Saying < is not antisymmetric because it lacks pairs — antisymmetry is vacuously satisfied when there are no qualifying pairs.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Thinking antisymmetric is the negation of symmetric — they're independent.
Treating relations as if they must be functions.
Forgetting that antisymmetry can be VACUOUSLY true.
Confusing the directed graph (arrow per pair) with an undirected graph.

flow.title: Property mnemonics
items: **Reflexive:** every element loves itself.
**Symmetric:** if A loves B, then B loves A.
**Antisymmetric:** mutual love only for self.
**Transitive:** love is contagious through friends.

sections.heading: Relations vs functions
sections.explanation: Relations are subsets of A × B; functions are special total single-valued relations.

sections.heading: Representations
sections.explanation: Directed graph, matrix, set of pairs.

step_by_step_solution: a ≤ a holds for every integer ✓.

quick_checks.question: Which property does '=' fail on ℤ?
quick_checks.explanation: Equality has reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.

quick_checks.question: Friendship on a social network is typically:
quick_checks.explanation: Friendship is mutual but not self-friending typically.

quick_checks.question: Antisymmetric is the opposite of symmetric.

key_takeaways: A relation on A is a subset of A × A.
Four core properties: reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.
= has all four; < has only antisymmetric (vacuously) and transitive.
Antisymmetric and symmetric are not opposites.
summary.next: Next: equivalence relations and partial orders — special combinations of these properties.

lessons.title: Equivalence Relations and Partial Orders
lessons.welcome: Two specific combinations of properties give us the most useful kinds of relations: EQUIVALENCE RELATIONS (which partition a set) and PARTIAL ORDERS (which generalize ≤).
objectives: Define an equivalence relation: reflexive + symmetric + transitive.
Identify equivalence classes and explain how they partition a set.
Define a partial order: reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive.
Distinguish partial orders from total (linear) orders.
Recognize Hasse diagrams for partial orders.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why are equivalence relations and partitions essentially the same?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Every equivalence relation on A partitions A into classes — sets of elements that are all equivalent to each other. Conversely, every partition defines an equivalence relation. The two views are interchangeable, and this is one of the most useful structural results in discrete math.

flow.title: Equivalence relation
flow.content: A relation R on A is an **equivalence relation** iff R is **reflexive, symmetric, AND transitive**. Examples: equality (=), congruence mod n, 'same KAU department as', 'same age as'.

flow.title: Equivalence class
flow.content: For a ∈ A, the **equivalence class** of a (under R) is `[a] = {x ∈ A | x R a}`. Two equivalence classes are either disjoint or identical. The collection of all equivalence classes **partitions** A.

flow.title: Equivalence relations and their classes
rows: Each integer is its own class
All students in section X form one class

flow.title: Equivalence around campus
items: **'Same Saudi region as'** on Saudi citizens: equivalence relation. Classes = the 13 regions.
**'Same CPCS 222 lab section as'**: equivalence on enrolled students. Classes = the lab sections.
**'Same area code as'** on STC numbers: equivalence relation.

flow.title: Partial order
flow.content: A relation R on A is a **partial order** iff R is **reflexive, antisymmetric, AND transitive**. The pair (A, R) is called a **partially ordered set** (poset). Standard example: ≤ on ℤ.

flow.title: Total (linear) order
flow.content: A partial order is a **total order** iff every pair of elements is **comparable**: ∀a, b ∈ A (a R b ∨ b R a). Examples: ≤ on ℝ. Non-example: subset (⊆) on P({1, 2}) — {1} and {2} are incomparable.

flow.trigger: After total orders — students often miss the comparability requirement.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Why isn't (ℤ⁺, |) a total order? It seems to relate everything.

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Because some pairs are incomparable. Take 2 and 3: neither divides the other. In a total order, EVERY pair must be related in one direction or the other. The divides relation is partial: it orders chains like 2 | 4 | 8 but leaves cousins like 2 and 3 unordered.

flow.title: Hasse diagram
flow.content: A **Hasse diagram** draws a finite poset compactly: it shows only the COVER relation (`a covers b` if a > b and there is no c strictly between). Reflexive loops and transitive shortcuts are omitted; the rest can be deduced. Lower elements are drawn below higher ones.

flow.title: Equivalence relation modulo 3
flow.problem: Show that 'a ≡ b (mod 3)' is an equivalence relation on ℤ and list the equivalence classes.
flow.thinking_process: Check the three properties; identify the residue classes.
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive: a - a = 0 = 3·0, so a ≡ a (mod 3). ✓
Symmetric: if a - b = 3k, then b - a = -3k = 3(-k). ✓
Transitive: a - b = 3k, b - c = 3m → a - c = 3(k + m). ✓
Three classes — the residues mod 3.
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting symmetry verification or listing wrong residues.

flow.title: Partial order check
flow.problem: Show that ⊆ on P({a, b, c}) is a partial order.
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive: every set X ⊆ X. ✓
Antisymmetric: X ⊆ Y and Y ⊆ X ⇒ X = Y (set equality). ✓
Transitive: X ⊆ Y and Y ⊆ Z ⇒ X ⊆ Z. ✓
Hence (P({a, b, c}), ⊆) is a poset.
flow.final_answer: Partial order. Not a total order (e.g., {a} and {b} are incomparable).
flow.common_mistake: Calling it a total order — totality requires that every pair be comparable.

flow.title: Building a partition
flow.problem: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, define R by 'same parity'. Find the partition.
flow.thinking_process: Equivalence classes are sets of elements with the same parity.
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive on parity. ✓
flow.common_mistake: Treating each element as its own class — they collapse into shared classes.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Calling a poset a total order without checking comparability.
Listing the same equivalence class twice — classes are sets, not labelled by the element.
Drawing reflexive loops and transitive shortcuts in a Hasse diagram (they should be omitted).
Confusing 'partial order' with 'partition'.

flow.title: Quick rules
items: **Equivalence relation = R + S + T.** Partitions the set.
**Partial order = R + AS + T.** Hasse diagrams.
**Total order = partial order + every pair comparable.**

sections.heading: Equivalence relations
sections.explanation: Reflexive + symmetric + transitive; classes partition the set.

sections.heading: Partial orders
sections.explanation: Reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive; may have incomparable pairs.

sections.heading: Total orders and Hasse diagrams
sections.explanation: Total = every pair comparable; Hasse diagrams compress partial orders visually.

worked_examples.problem: Is 'same age as' an equivalence relation?
step_by_step_solution: Reflexive ✓, symmetric ✓, transitive ✓. Yes.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Confusing same-age with same-birth-year (equivalent on a given day, but loose over time).

quick_checks.question: Which is an equivalence relation on ℤ?
Every equivalence relation gives a partition.

key_takeaways: Equivalence = reflexive + symmetric + transitive; classes partition the set.
Total order requires every pair to be comparable.
Hasse diagrams represent partial orders compactly.

questions.explanation: A friend of a friend is not necessarily your friend.

questions.question: Following on X is symmetric.
Define equivalence relation.
questions.answer: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

questions.question: List the equivalence classes of ≡ (mod 4) on ℤ.
Why is divides (|) on ℤ⁺ a partial order but not total?
questions.answer: Reflexive (a | a), antisymmetric (a | b and b | a ⇒ a = b on ℤ⁺), transitive (a | b and b | c ⇒ a | c). Not total: 2 ∤ 3 and 3 ∤ 2.

questions.question: How does a Hasse diagram differ from a directed graph of a partial order?
questions.answer: Omits reflexive loops and transitive shortcuts; orients top-to-bottom.

questions.question: Why do equivalence classes partition a set?
questions.answer: Two classes are either equal or disjoint (by symmetry+transitivity); every element is in some class (by reflexivity). Together: partition.

questions.question: Equivalence = R + ___ + T.
Partial order = ___ + AS + T.
Total order adds: every pair is ___.
Equivalence class of a: [a] = {x | x R ___}.
On ℤ, mod-n has ___ equivalence classes.
Match relation to type.
On A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, R = {(1,1), (1,2), (2,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4)}. Check the four properties.
questions.answer:
Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) ∈ R ✓.
Symmetric: (1,2), (2,1) both in R ✓.
Antisymmetric: (1,2) and (2,1) both in R but 1 ≠ 2 ✗.
Transitive: (1,2)·(2,1)→(1,1) ✓; (2,1)·(1,2)→(2,2) ✓ ✓.
Reflexive ✓, Symmetric ✓, Antisymmetric ✗, Transitive ✓.

questions.question: Show ≡ (mod 4) on ℤ is an equivalence relation.
questions.answer:
Reflexive: 4 | 0 = a - a. ✓
Symmetric: 4 | (a-b) ⇒ 4 | -(a-b) = b - a. ✓
Transitive: 4 | (a-b) and 4 | (b-c) ⇒ 4 | (a-c). ✓
Equivalence classes: [0], [1], [2], [3] (four residues).

questions.question: Decide if (ℤ⁺, |) is a partial order.
questions.answer:
Reflexive: a | a (any a divides itself). ✓
Antisymmetric: a | b and b | a on ℤ⁺ ⇒ a = b. ✓
Transitive: a | b and b | c ⇒ a | c. ✓
Partial order. Not total (2 and 3 incomparable).

questions.question: Define R on people: a R b iff a and b have the same student ID. Is R an equivalence relation? Describe the classes.
questions.answer: Reflexive (every person has their own ID and shares it with themselves), symmetric, transitive. Equivalence relation. Classes: each person forms their own class (assuming unique IDs).
questions.explanation: Each person is unique — singleton classes.

questions.question: Show that the cover-relation '⋖' (a ⋖ b iff a < b and no c between) need NOT be transitive in (ℤ⁺, ≤).
questions.answer: 1 ⋖ 2 (no integer strictly between). 2 ⋖ 3. But 1 ⋖ 3 fails because 2 lies between. So 1 ⋖ 2 and 2 ⋖ 3, yet ¬(1 ⋖ 3).
questions.explanation: Cover is not transitive — that's why Hasse diagrams use cover edges only.

questions.question: If R and S are both equivalence relations on A, is R ∩ S an equivalence relation?
questions.answer: Yes. Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R, (a, a) ∈ S → (a, a) ∈ R ∩ S. Symmetric/transitive checks similar via intersection. ∎

questions.question: On a class, define 'sits in same row as'. Equivalence relation? What are the classes?
questions.answer: Reflexive ✓, symmetric ✓, transitive ✓. Yes. Classes = the rows of the classroom.

questions.template: Decide if {REL} is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.
questions.example_realization: a < b on ℤ → R ✗, S ✗, AS ✓ (vacuous), T ✓.

questions.instructions: Total iff every pair is comparable.
